articles.title: Mamdani says wealthy donors killed California’s billionaire tax — but Americans aren't done forcing the rich to pay up
articles.summary: "There were other ballot referendums that took place across the country calling for what is essentially the same thing."
articles.body:
California voters may have rejected a one-time tax on billionaires, but New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said that vote alone tells us little about how Americans feel about taxing the rich.

Speaking at The New York Times' DealBook Summit on Nov. 22, Mamdani said opponents spent heavily to defeat Proposition 40 in California. He then pointed to other states where voters approved higher taxes on wealthy people.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 5 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

"There were other ballot referendums that took place across the country calling for what is essentially the same thing, which is higher taxes on the wealthiest," Mamdani said, according to the Times .

In New York, the democratic socialist mayor has clashed with some of Wall Street's biggest names over his own push to raise taxes on wealthy New Yorkers.

California's Proposition 40 would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of residents worth more than $1 billion, with most of the money going to healthcare. The measure lost with 52% of voters voting against it.

One committee fighting the tax raised more than $333 million, with major donations from Google co-founder Sergey Brin and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt. Gov. Gavin Newsom also opposed the measure.

Critics, meanwhile, warned that it could drive billionaires out of California and cost the state income tax revenue. California's top 1% of earners paid nearly 37% of the state's personal income taxes in 2023, according to the governor's 2026–27 budget summary.

"I don't think you're going to see such a good Democratic electorate in the near future," Wesley Hussey, a political science professor at California State University in Sacramento, told the Associated Press . "This was the time to pass something that was pretty lefty and progressive and had a lot of opposition."

In New York, Mamdani took his case for taxing the rich straight to the front door of one of the wealthiest people in the city. "Well, today, we're taxing the rich," Mamdani said in a video filmed outside the Manhattan building where hedge fund billionaire Ken Griffin owns a penthouse.

articles.title: Motociclistas que dão grau e postam na internet são alvos de operação | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo o Ministério Público, grupo usava redes sociais para divulgar, promover e incentivar manobras. Armas, celulares, munições e motos também foram apreendidos.
articles.summary: Operação contra grau no ES prende três em flagrante e suspende 16 habilitações após investigação de manobras perigosas divulgadas em redes sociais em Linhares.
articles.body:
Três pessoas são presas em operação que investiga suspeitos de manobras irregulares com motocicletas no Espírito Santo — Foto: Divulgação/MPES

Três pessoas foram presas em flagrante durante uma operação voltada ao combate de manobras perigosas com motocicletas, conhecidas como "grau", em Linhares , no Norte do Espírito Santo, na manhã desta terça-feira (24).

Além das prisões, foram apreendidos celulares, armas, munições, motos, peças automotivas, materiais de divulgação e troféus utilizados em manobras.

Ao todo, 16 mandados de busca e apreensão foram cumpridos. Segundo o Ministério Público do Espírito Santo (MPES), o grupo usava redes sociais para divulgar, promover e incentivar as manobras.

De acordo com as investigações, desenvolvidas a partir do setor de Inteligência da Guarda Civil Municipal de Linhares, foram identificados indícios da atuação recorrente e articulada de motociclistas na realização de manobras de risco.

A Justiça do Espírito Santo deferiu medidas cautelares de suspensão da permissão ou da habilitação para dirigir, além da suspensão das redes sociais utilizadas para a divulgação das manobras. Segundo balanço do MPES, 16 motociclistas tiveram a habilitação suspensa e 18 perfis nas redes sociais serão derrubados.

A operação abrange investigados nos municípios de Linhares, Sooretama e São Gabriel da Palha , também no Norte do estado. As idades e nomes dos detidos não foram divulgados.

Para chegar aos suspeitos, foi feita uma análise de imagens do sistema de videomonitoramento municipal e de redes sociais. A partir desse monitoramento, foi possível identificar condutores, motocicletas e perfis digitais utilizados para as práticas.

Durante as diligências, também foram identificadas motocicletas com modificações irregulares, como escapamentos adulterados, ausência de retrovisores e dispositivos destinados a dificultar a identificação das placas.

Para o MPES, além de elementos para o esclarecimento dos fatos e a eventual responsabilização dos envolvidos, a atuação tem caráter preventivo, contribuindo para a proteção das pessoas que utilizam as vias da região.

As condutas investigadas podem caracterizar crimes previstos no Código de Trânsito Brasileiro, sem prejuízo da apuração de outras infrações.

Peças de motocicletas também foram apreendidas durante operação que prendeu três pessoas no ES — Foto: Divulgação/MPES

articles.title: Coast Guard boards 2 foreign ships bound for US amid reports of Iranian hacking probe
articles.summary: U.S. Coast Guard cyber teams boarded two foreign vessels in the Gulf of America after their networks were compromised by foreign cyber actors at sea.
articles.body: The U.S. Coast Guard deployed specialized cyber teams to board two foreign-flagged commercial ships bound for U.S. ports in August after indications that their networks had been compromised by "foreign cyber actors," a Coast Guard spokesperson told Fox News Digital on Monday. The offshore operations took place Aug. 21 and 24 in the Gulf of America, with teams mitigating the threats before the vessels reached U.S. ports. The confirmation came as The Wall Street Journal also reported Monday that U.S. authorities are investigating whether Iran was involved in dozens of cyberattacks targeting energy tankers. FEARS OF CHINA SPYING ON US MILITARY PROMPT GOP HAWKS TO DEMAND RETALIATION AGAINST THE SHIPPING GIANT "The U.S. Coast Guard (USCG), in close coordination with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and federal cybersecurity experts, recently conducted joint offshore security boardings of two inbound foreign-flagged commercial vessels in the Gulf of America," a Coast Guard spokesperson said. "The measures were designed to ensure the integrity of the vessel’s operational and information technology systems following indications that the networks of both vessels were compromised by foreign cyber actors." The Coast Guard said a specialized team of law enforcement personnel, Coast Guard Cyber Protection Team members, a vessel inspector and FBI Cyber Action Team operators boarded the first vessel Aug. 21 to investigate the suspected cybersecurity breach. "The captain, crew and shore-side corporate staff were critical partners in helping to ensure the threats were mitigated," the spokesperson added. A similar multiagency boarding and safety verification operation was conducted Aug. 24 aboard the second vessel, also in the Gulf of America, the Coast Guard said. FRENCH SUPERMARKETS FACE MILLIONS IN LOSSES AFTER CYBERATTACK HITS REFRIGERATORS NATIONWIDE No operational disruptions, vessel instability, threats to crew safety or environmental impacts have been reported. The Coast Guard said it is coordinating with port operators, vessel owners and local maritime stakeholders to ensure port operations continue safely and without interruption. According to The Wall Street Journal, attackers exploited vulnerabilities in Fortinet networking equipment, prompting Coast Guard boardings after crews received bomb threats warning that "traitor ships will burn in hell." STRAIT OF HORMUZ CRISIS TRAPS 6,000 SAILORS AS ATTACKS ON SHIPS MOUNT, UN MARITIME CHIEF SAYS As many as 50 vessels carrying oil, liquefied petroleum, chemicals and other potentially explosive cargo are believed to have been targeted, the outlet reported, citing U.S. officials. A European shipping executive also said officers received threats on their cellphones. A ransom letter addressed to the captain of the Liberian-flagged supertanker Prosperity, which was carrying about 2.3 million barrels of oil, described the operation as a "planned execution." Hackers reportedly breached one vessel's propulsion and navigation systems, disrupting communications for about 30 hours and forcing the crew to switch to manual procedures, potentially delaying energy shipments to Asia and Europe. AMERICA MUST DEFEND OUR DIGITAL INFRASTRUCTURE, HERE AND OVERSEAS, TO WIN THE NEXT WAR "The Marine Transportation System is vital to America's economic prosperity and national security, and safeguarding it against potential cyber risks is a standard part of the United States Coast Guard's safety and security mission," the Coast Guard spokesperson said. "Just as we monitor for mechanical or weather-related hazards, we incorporate cyber risk management into our routine, professional approach to facilitating commerce and ensuring safe vessel transits into and from our ports and waterways. "While confirmed cyber disruptions in the maritime domain remain uncommon, even isolated technical issues can cause avoidable commercial delays. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We encourage all maritime stakeholders to leverage Coast Guard Cyber Command’s free, non-regulatory technical resources to maintain strong digital hygiene and report any suspected anomalies to the National Response Center," the spokesperson added.

articles.title: Army wants to resume helicopter flights near Reagan National airport
articles.summary: The Army is seeking federal approval to resume helicopter training flights near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, drawing safety concerns nearly two years after a deadly midair collision over the Potomac River killed 67 people. Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.), whose district includes the airport, said Monday that Army officials informed his office during a briefing…
articles.body:
The Army is seeking federal approval to resume helicopter training flights near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, drawing safety concerns nearly two years after a deadly midair collision over the Potomac River killed 67 people.

Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.), whose district includes the airport, said Monday that Army officials informed his office during a briefing that they had contacted the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) about restarting the flights and were awaiting a response.

“Army officials assured my office that no flights will take place unless they are approved by the FAA,” Beyer wrote in a post on the social platform X . “While Army officials further committed to implementing all NTSB [National Transportation Safety Board] safety recommendations, it is clear that this work is not complete.”

He continued, “The path forward must prioritize safety, and that requires full implementation of the NTSB’s recommendations before training flights resume.”

An Army spokesperson told Politico on Monday that the military hopes to restart the flights as early as the second week of December. Army officials also briefed staff on the Senate Commerce and Armed Services committees last week, according to the outlet.

The FAA told Politico on Friday that it had not received a formal request to restart the flights and reiterated Monday that the Army would need the agency’s approval before training could resume.

Federal regulators imposed restrictions on helicopter traffic near Reagan National Airport near Washington, D.C., after an Army Black Hawk helicopter collided with an American Airlines regional passenger jet in January 2025, killing everyone aboard both aircrafts.

The FAA suspended military helicopter training flights in the area in May of that year after another Black Hawk flew too close to the airport, prompting air traffic controllers to divert commercial flights.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called the incident “unacceptable” at the time and vowed to press Pentagon officials on “why the hell our rules were disregarded.”

Lawmakers announced a practical agreement on aviation safety legislation intended to prevent another deadly collision. Negotiations have centered in part on requirements for military aircrafts to use surveillance technology that would improve pilots’ awareness of any nearby aircrafts.

The Army’s own investigation into the fatal collision produced more than 30 recommendations, including changes to air traffic control procedures and better coordination with the FAA.

articles.title: Army proceeding with lead detonation on Wednesday
articles.summary: The Army is going ahead with detonating lead-containing munitions in Iowa on Wednesday after President Trump threw additional uncertainty into the controversy on Monday. “We are proceeding with the controlled removal in full coordination with all state, local and federal authorities, because the safety of Iowa’s citizens comes first,” said acting Army Secretary Adam Telle…
articles.body:
The Army is going ahead with detonating lead-containing munitions in Iowa on Wednesday after President Trump threw additional uncertainty into the controversy on Monday.

“We are proceeding with the controlled removal in full coordination with all state, local and federal authorities, because the safety of Iowa’s citizens comes first,” said acting Army Secretary Adam Telle in a post on X.

Telle said moving forward was a “consensus decision.”

“Every expert agency agrees, and both Iowa’s current and incoming Governors say the call belongs to the experts,” he wrote, also noting that a federal appeals court declined to block an emergency permit for controlled explosion on Monday.

The Army announced last week that it planned to detonate degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, in a matter of days — resulting in a plume with lead-containing particles in the air.

The announcement created an uproar, causing fears that people would be exposed to toxic lead both immediately and in the aftermath. The federal government has argued that doing a controlled detonation would be more favorable than risking an accidental explosion. The saga has also raised questions about why the situation is happening in the first place.

The detonation had been slated for Monday, but on Sunday, the Army said it would actually be postponed until Wednesday “to allow for more optimal weather conditions.”

However, Trump on Monday said the Army would only go ahead with agreement from the court and Gov.-elect Rob Sand (D).

Sand later said that the administration should make the decision.

In children, exposure to lead can cause brain damage, nervous system damage, learning problems, behavioral issues and a lower IQ. In rare cases, it can also cause seizures, coma and death, according to the Environmental Protection Agency.

In adults, lead exposure can cause decreased kidney function, heart-related issues and fertility issues.

articles.title: AI market whipsaw puts Kevin Warsh's rate-hike strategy to the test
articles.summary: With Warsh silent during the market's recent swings, investors are parsing both the divided commentary from his colleagues and the clues he left behind at hi...
articles.body:
When stocks tanked last week, Wall Street briefly bet the Federal Reserve would ease up on interest rate hikes. Now Monday's massive rebound — sparked by Jensen Huang's reinstatement at Nvidia — has revived bets on at least two more interest rate hikes.

Yet with AI stocks still off their highs, the sector's volatility is emerging as a critical test for Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh and the central bank's path for rate hikes.

"AI stress is not mostly due to the Fed. But it is not a coincidence it is occurring when the Fed is hiking," said Krishna Guha, head of central banking and the economy for Evercore ISI. "Talk of 50-basis-point hikes or faster tightening adds to stress. Fed Chair Warsh not talking is a problem. It leaves the market guessing: Is he a hardcore hawk or a market-sensitive hawk? The gap is filled by others whose views can lag the leadership."

"This is a serious test for Warsh," Guha added.

With Warsh silent during the market's recent swings, investors are parsing both the divided commentary from his colleagues and the clues he left behind at his late-October press conference.

Last week, Fed officials offered competing visions for how aggressively to move. Fed governor Chris Waller said that if the central bank hikes by a quarter point next month, it will need to signal a follow-up hike of the same size in January — or else deliver a jumbo half-percentage-point increase in December . Fed governor Lisa Cook echoed that urgency on Friday, right as the market hit its nadir. Arguing that financial conditions remain too accommodative while inflation stays stubbornly high, she warned the central bank risks falling behind the curve if it doesn't hike now.

New York Fed president John Williams, however, pushed back against calls for supersize rate hikes , saying last week that he doesn't think the situation calls for "dramatic action."

For his part, Warsh staked out a middle-ground framework following the Fed's decision to hold rates steady on Oct. 28 — three-and-a-half weeks before the tech rout. While noting that overall financial and credit conditions had tightened since September's rate hike, he stopped short of calling them "tight." Crucially, he also signaled he is watching the AI sector closely , noting that credit spreads had widened for certain assets and acknowledging that interest rates are not "somehow divorced" from the AI investment surge.

Now, Wall Street is divided over whether Warsh's focus on financial conditions will restrain the central bank, or if his inflation target will force him to keep hiking into a fragile market.

articles.title: Too young to be vaccinated for measles? Babies face growing threats from outbreaks
articles.summary: As measles outbreaks continue to soar, a new question has emerged: Should doctors give measles shots earlier to better protect babies?
articles.body:
As measles outbreaks continue to soar nationwide, increasingly spilling from small, close-knit communities into the general population, a new question has emerged: Should doctors give measles shots earlier to better protect babies?

Dr. Kristen Panthagani, an emergency medicine doctor in Connecticut, is worried about her baby, who has just turned 6 months old — too young for the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine that's given after age 1.

"I've been trying to figure out what to do to protect my son," Panthagani said on her public health blog, called " You can know things ." He's "in a tricky period when it comes to measles. He's in a window of vulnerability where he likely doesn't have protection against the virus."

Babies are born with antibodies against measles if their mothers have been vaccinated. But new evidence shows that protection doesn't last as long as previously thought.

"The assumption has always been that up until 6 months of age, babies are protected, and then from 6 to 12 months, there's some waning," said Dr. Buddy Creech, a pediatric infectious disease specialist and director of the Vanderbilt Vaccine Research Program at Vanderbilt University Medical Center. "That's why we give the vaccine at 12 months."

New research from Creech's team shows that protection is gone long before a child's first birthday. Researchers analyzed blood samples from 92 mother-infant pairs and found that less than 20% of 6-month-old babies still have those protective antibodies.

"By somewhere between 4 to 6 months of age, the majority of kids have completely lost the level of seroprotection that would be needed to protect against measles," Creech said. He presented the research at an October meeting of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. It's not been peer-reviewed.

For more on the measles outbreak, read The Vaccine Divide , a data investigation into how the deadly virus is roaring back and childhood vaccine defenses continue to crack and crumble.

Now that cases have exploded in the U.S., babies in that 6- to 11-month window are increasingly defenseless against the virus.

"We're going to have to rethink when we should give the first dose of measles vaccine," Creech said.

When should kids get their measles shots?

For decades, the guidance was straightforward: Children receive their first MMR shot at 12 to 15 months old, followed by a second dose between ages 4 and 6. Together, the shots are 97% effective at protecting against measles, usually for life.

In areas with active outbreaks, however, babies at 6 months old can get an early or "zero" MMR shot ahead of their two regular doses.

And toddlers who've already had their first regular dose don't have to wait until age 4 for their second shot. They're eligible for the second dose 28 days after their first for maximum protection.

Many parents in outbreak areas have taken advantage of the change in guidance. "We have seen huge uptake in the zero dose as well as in the early second dose," Pennsylvania Secretary of Health Dr. Debra Bogen said last week during a briefing with the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials. More than 67,000 early MMR shots have been given in Pennsylvania since July, according to the state health department .

The growing question now is whether those exceptions should become more widely used — or whether the routine vaccination schedule itself needs reconsideration — now that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status.

"There are people looking at this right now. They're reviewing all of the latest science and seeing if the recommendation should change," said Dr. Deanna Behrens, a Chicago-area pediatrician and secretary of the Illinois chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics. "We are on high alert."

As of Friday, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had confirmed 5,838 cases , though the number is likely a vast undercount. More than 1,000 of those cases have been in kids under 5. About 17% of those children have needed hospitalization.

Most kids recover from measles without a problem. But as the virus has caught fire across the U.S., doctors in outbreak zones have reported severe complications in some children , including trouble breathing, severe dehydration, pneumonia and brain swelling. Babies with measles are also at greater risk of developing a condition called subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE, years after their infection. It's almost always fatal.

Twelve people have died of measles this year, according to state health departments. At least half of those deaths have been in babies or toddlers.

The Vaccine Integrity Project, part of the University of Minnesota's Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy, recently summarized the latest data on zero doses of MMR vaccine. The shot is 58% effective when given between 6 and 9 months, and 83% between 9 and 11 months.

Side effects from the shots, such as fever and, rarely, febrile seizures, were the same in younger and older children.

But there's also evidence, the Vaccine Integrity Project's review found, that the zero dose may impact how well kids' immune systems respond to the two routinely recommended MMR shots.

"It's a trade-off right now," said Dr. Heidi Moline, a pediatrician and clinical adviser to the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy. "When there's a significant amount of measles virus circulating, the short-term benefit of protection against measles outweighs the long-term lower antibodies."

As of now, there's no indication the CDC is considering changes to the childhood vaccine schedule. The AAP said the group will review all of its immunization recommendations early next year. The CDC didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Vaccines recommended by the CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices are generally free. There have been reports of health insurance claims being denied for early MMR vaccination, according to the AAP.

"This is something the vaccine policy people are really going to have to look at," said Dr. Peter Hotez, co-director of the Texas Children's Hospital Center for Vaccine Development.

articles.title: TSA detects suspicious movement in traveler’s suitcase during security screening
articles.summary: A TSA officer at Ontario International Airport spotted suspicious movement in a traveler's luggage and found live snakes, including a rattlesnake, inside a checked bag. An expert weighed in.
articles.body: TSA officers at California’s Ontario International Airport (ONT) recently faced an alarming situation while screening a checked bag. During a routine bag inspection, TSA Officer Benjamin Andrade-Carillo spotted suspicious movement in a pillowcase. Initially, the shape inside the pillowcase appeared stringy, like a rope. But on closer inspection, the officer saw that the object was moving, according to an employee story published on the agency’s website. TSA OFFICER SEES ALARMING SHAPES ON X-RAY BEFORE STOLEN CIVIL WAR MYSTERY UNRAVELS The officer removed the pillowcase from the bag and quickly determined it was not rope. "When I realized the item in my hand was alive, I told myself, ‘I need to escalate this immediately,’" Andrade-Carillo said, the TSA's website noted. Andrade-Carillo notified his supervisory officer, Suggey Flores. "I felt it tense up and start moving," Flores said. SHARP WEAPON DISCOVERED BY TSA TUCKED INSIDE UNUSUAL ITEM IN PASSENGER'S CARRY-ON BAG "I have held snakes before, so I wasn’t too spooked. I was more impressed," he added, "because it’s not something you see every day." Flores informed the ONT TSA manager, Francisco "Frank" Calderon, as well as airport police and the airline about the find. Calderon confirmed there were live snakes inside the pillowcase and that one was a rattlesnake. "TSA officers should not be handling live snakes for safety reasons," Calderon said. "Our priority was ensuring the safety of our officers and everyone in the area while making the proper notifications and coordinating a safe resolution," according to the TSA. "I felt it tense up and start moving." Due to safety reasons, the immediate area was vacated. "Safety was a concern because we didn’t know what kind of snakes they were," Flores said. "They could have been venomous." BIZARRE X-RAY SCAN LEADS TSA OFFICERS TO FLIGHT PASSENGER'S ILLEGAL STASH The flyer removed the snakes and gave them to a non-traveling family member. TSA then re-screened the luggage and permitted the traveler to fly. Fox News Digital reached out to the agency for more information. "The transportation of live reptiles is not automatically prohibited, but acceptance of venomous species is much more restrictive for airlines," Keith Jeffries of Florida, vice president of K2 Security Screening Group and a former federal security director for TSA at Los Angeles International Airport, told Fox News Digital. The traveler said the snakes were pets, according to the Los Angeles TSA Coordination Center. He also said he had previously traveled with the snakes on another airline. "I've seen cases with birds, turtles, snakes. I mean, it's just never-ending." "The basic rule is you need to [give] plenty of advance notice if you're shipping those types of items," said Jeffries. "You have got to have the proper containers. You've got to have the warning labels, the documentation for the permits to transport it." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER He went on, "Then, of course, you've got to have somebody that specializes in handling that type of cargo that's properly trained. They look for the environmental conditions and the safe loading and unloading of those types of animals." "In my two years of service, I had not found anything like this," Andrade-Carillo said in the employee story on the TSA site. "In San Diego, I experienced a gentleman trying to bring live lobsters as a carry-on." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES "We ask the traveling public to be mindful of what they bring in their bags," he also said, "because if we don’t know what it is, we will find out." "I am very happy with the way our team handled the situation, stopped screening when they needed to and made the proper notifications," Calderon said. "No injuries or bites were reported, thank goodness." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Jason Pantages, the TSA’s federal security director for Los Angeles International and surrounding airports, agreed with that assessment. "This incident demonstrates the sound judgment and teamwork of the ONT TSA workforce as well as the importance of travelers checking with their airline before bringing animals, including reptiles, to the airport," said Pantages on the TSA's site. "I've seen cases with birds, turtles, snakes before. I mean, it's just never-ending," Jeffries told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It's not that they're trying to wreak havoc on a security system," he added. At times, flyers are just "trying to make a buck. It's [as] simple as that."

articles.title: Kalshi halts trading in Utah.
articles.summary:
The prediction market platform paused operations after a federal court ruled that Utah can enforce state gambling laws, according to The Salt Lake Tribune. Kalshi is also waiting on the outcome of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s (CFTC) legal battle against Utah, which aims to block the state’s attempts to regulate prediction markets.
[Link: After judge signals ‘steep hill’ in regulatory case, Kalshi pauses operations in Utah | https://www.sltrib.com/news/2026/11/23/kalshi-pauses-operations-utah-amid/ | The Salt Lake Tribune]
articles.body:
Everything is gambling now: the latest news on prediction markets like Polymarket and Kalshi

The prediction market platform paused operations after a federal court ruled that Utah can enforce state gambling laws, according to The Salt Lake Tribune . Kalshi is also waiting on the outcome of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s (CFTC) legal battle against Utah, which aims to block the state’s attempts to regulate prediction markets.
